ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Sustainable bio-based adhesive is a promising substitute for petroleum-based adhesives to alleviate serious environmental and health problems. In this work, a nanoengineered starch-based adhesive was fabricated by grafting vinyl acetate (VAc) onto starch molecule and subsequently incorporating the functional nanoparticle [TiO2-coupling-poly(butyl acrylate, BA), TKB] to overcome the drawbacks present in conventional nanocomposite adhesive. Results showed that the presence of BA altered the surface property of TKB, leading to improved dispersion. In the adhesive with 4% (mass ratio to starch) TKB, TKB aggregates played the role as a sliding bridge, which significantly promoted the storage stability and shear strength in both dry and wet states. Additionally, the latex film with 4% TKB exhibited high compatibility and water resistance due to the promoted hydrophobicity. This study provides a fundamental insight into the improvement of functional nanoparticles on the performance of starch-based adhesive, suggesting a novel strategy for designing high-performance bio-adhesive.

ce:section.ce:para: Adhesive is a common product in the chemical industry, which has been widely used in the furniture and building industries. Over the past decade, owing to the global energy crisis and health problems, petroleum-based adhesives are not eco-friendly, facilitating the development of adhesives based on the sustainable and non-toxic resource (e.g. cellulose, soy protein, starch, others) (Droesbeke et al., 2020; Monroy et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). The abundant availability of starch combined with its excellent properties, such as renewability, biodegradation, and low cost, makes it suitable for the preparation of bio-based adhesive. However, the low bonding performance and stability of starch-based adhesives limit its application in the fast-developing adhesive industry. Therefore, many techniques for starch modification have been evaluated to improve the relevant properties of the starch-based adhesive, such as gelatinization, oxidation, grafting polymerization, and cross-linking modification (Din et al., 2020). However, unsatisfactory bonding performance still restricts the utilization of adhesive in the plywood industry.

Nanoparticles, as a kind of non-covalent cross-linking agent, can facilitate the formation of macromolecular network structure (Cheng et al., 2019). This makes it popular in the adhesive system to improve the structure and compatibility between different components. Previous reports have confirmed that nanoparticles could improve the bonding performances of bio-based wood adhesive. For examples, Wang et al. (2011) prepared the starch-based wood adhesive with high dry shear strength by incorporating 10% untreated silica; Li et al. (2015) reported that 5% montmorillonite nanoparticles could improve the dry and wet shear strength by 80.3% and 90.0% respectively; Qiao et al. (2014) fabricated a composite starch-based adhesive, and 0.357% (with respect to the solution mass) carboxymethyl cellulose was found to enhance the bonding strength. Similar work was performed by our research group using 4% nano-TiO2 that significantly promoted the dry and wet shear strength of starch-based wood adhesive (Chen et al., 2018). These results proved that nanoparticles could enhance the molecular rigidity of grafted starch by forming a highly resistant structure. However, the rapid increase in viscosity (up to 20 Pa·s) in 30 days storage period limited its practical application. This viscosity-promoting effect of inorganic nanoparticles also occurred in other nanocomposites, such as the bio-based film containing nanoparticles which showed a decrease in elongation at break (Oleyaei et al., 2016; Shaili et al., 2015). High structural rigidity is sometimes not conducive to the application of soft matter, especially during plasticity and storage. Therefore, techniques to overcome this drawback caused by adding inorganic nanoparticles are necessary.

Hydrophobic modification of the surface might be a promising strategy to solve this problem as previous studies have reported that polymer grafted (PG) nanoparticles functioned similar to surfactants and showed a high dispersion rate in composite systems (Akcora et al., 2009; Maillard et al., 2011). Recently, various kinds of PG nanoparticles have been developed for controlling the dispersion into a polymer matrix (Shen et al., 2019; Moll et al., 2011). According to these reports, PG nanoparticles could aggregate in anisotropic structures with different shapes (e.g. strings, sheets, or connected structures). This phenomenon was related to the balance between the core-core interaction and distribution of polymer segments on the particle surface (Tang & Arya, 2017). Besides, these nanoparticle aggregates also possess different surface properties, which might be critical to explain their interaction with the polymer (Lu et al., 2021). In previous literature (Nugent et al., 2010), several materials with PG nanoparticles displayed the liquid-like behavior, directly proving a different role of PG nanoparticles in soft material, which might be related to the two network scenarios (“particle-only” and “particle-polymer”) (Kumar et al., 2013). Therefore, PG nanoparticles are proposed to be applied in the starch-based wood adhesive.

For PG nanoparticles, the selection of grafted polymer is also important. Previously, a starch-based adhesive was prepared by grafting vinyl acetate (VAc)-co-butyl acrylate (BA) onto the starch chain, and results demonstrated that the introduction of BA could significantly improve the bonding performance and latex dispersion (Din et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018). Moreover, the rice straw fiber modified by poly butyl acrylate (PBA) was concluded to enhance the tensile strength and elongation at break of polymer composite (Qin et al., 2011). These results suggested the availability of BA in the adhesive based on starch-g-poly(VAc).

Accordingly, a sustainable starch-based adhesive was fabricated by incorporating the polymer grafted nano-TiO2 (TKB) which was synthesized through the coupling and grafting polymerization (Scheme 1 ). Subsequently, the structure of TKB was characterized, and the relevant properties and morphology of the adhesive were investigated to reveal the interaction mechanism between the TKB particles and latex. This research provides a novel strategy of incorporating the designed functional nanoparticles for preparing high-performance sustainable starch-based adhesive, which could be attractive for a wide range of plywood industries.

Corn starch [moisture content, 12%; amylose content, 27% (w/w, dry basis); protein%, 0.40% (w/w, dry basis); purity>99%] were provided by Hebei Langfang Starch Co., Ltd. (Hebei, China). Saline coupling agents (C10H20O5Si, γ-methacryloxypropyl trimethoxy silane; KH570; purity, 97%) were obtained from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Nano-titanium dioxide (nano-TiO2, 99.8%, 60 nm, anatase) was purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation (Shanghai, China). Absolute ethanol (CH3-CH2OH), calcium chloride (CaCl2), butyl acrylate (CH2 = CHCOO(CH2)3CH3, BA), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3), vinyl acetate (CH3COOCH=CH2, VAc), ammonium persulfate (APS), sodium dodecylsulfate (SDS), polyvinyl alcohol (PVA; DP = 1750 ± 50, alcoholysis degree>99%) and Acetone (C3H6O, CAS:67-64-1) were supplied by Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Hydrochloric acid (HCl; purity, 36–38%) was provided by Xin Yang Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. (Henan, China). All reagents were of chemical grade.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Surface modification of nano-TiO2 by KH570
ce:section.ce:para: The method was designed according to several previous references with some modifications (Halder et al., 2015; Li et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2013). The unmodified TiO2 nanoparticles were first dried in a vacuum oven at 50 °C for about 24 h to remove the residual water. Subsequently, 10 g dry TiO2 nanoparticles were dispersed in 50 mL absolute ethanol, followed by high-speed shear dispersion for 5 min. Then, 70% [w% = w(KH570)/w(TiO2)%] KH570 was added into the slurry and treated with ultrasonic (30 kHz) for 15 min. Next, the mixture was kept in a water bath with magnetic stirring and stirred at 50 °C for 2 h. Finally, this mixture was filtered under atmospheric pressure (filter paper is qualitative filter paper) and washed by using ethanol for 4 times to remove the residual KH570 and dried in a vacuum oven at 50 °C for 24 h to obtain the modified nano-TiO2 (TiO2-KH570; TK) powder.

The 10 g dry TK particles and 1 g SDS were first dispersed into the distilled water, and this slurry was treated with ultrasonic (30 kHz) for 10 min. This slurry was subsequently poured into a four-necked round-bottomed flask in a water bath at 70 °C with continuous stirring. Then, 0.1 g APS (APS should be added into water to prepare APS/Water, w/w = 10%, solution) was added into the suspension, followed by adding 20 mL BA dropwise within 2 h, then maintained for another 30 min. Next, the latex in the reaction mixture was precipitated by the 5 w% CaCl2 aqueous solution and then filtered, washed by ethanol for 4 times. TiO2-KH570-PBA (TKB) particles were finally obtained after freeze-drying and soxhlet extraction (Acetone, 70 °C for 48 h).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of the starch-based wood adhesives and grafted starch containing different percentage of TKB particles
ce:section.ce:para: The adhesives and copolymers were prepared based on our previous report (Chen et al., 2018). 50 g of corn starch and 120 mL of hydrochloric acid (HCl, 0.5 M) were mixed in a four-necked round-bottomed flask and stirred for 120 min at 60 °C. The pH was adjusted to neutral by using sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 10 M). Next, the temperature was increased to 85 °C and maintained for 30 min to gelatinize. Then, the reaction temperature was reduced to 60 °C, followed by the addition of 2 g SDS (surfactant), 15 mL VAc, TKB (0%, 2%, 4%, 6%, 8%, w/w, corn starch basis) and 0.3 g APS (APS should be mixed with 3 mL distilled water for preparing 10% solution). Next, the pH was adjusted to 4–5 with hydrochloric acid (HCl, 0.5 M). After 30 min of initiation reaction, the temperature was raised to 70 °C. Meanwhile, residual 45 mL of vinyl acetate was slowly added into the suspension over a period of 2.5 h and kept for 30 min. Following this, the temperature was increased to 80 °C and maintained for 30 min. Finally, the adhesive was cooled to 30 °C, and the pH was then adjusted to 6.

To obtain the grafted starch, the starch-g-PVAc emulsion should be prepared according to the above description but without adding PVA. The suspension was then precipitated with ethanol and washed with distilled water for 4 times by centrifugation. The solids in the bottom of the centrifuge tube should be freeze-dried to obtain a powder mixture. Finally, the powder sample was extracted with acetone by soxhlet extraction (70 °C for 72 h) to completely remove homopolymers of VAc monomers.

ce:section.ce:section-title: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (H-TEM) and particle size distribution measurement
ce:section.ce:para: The microstructure of the TiO2 and TKB particles was observed by the H-TEM method. The powder samples were respectively dispersed in absolute ethanol, and the suspension was treated by an ultrasonic generator for 20 min. After that, this suspension was dropped onto the copper grid to dry. The size distribution of TiO2 and TKB particles was also measured by a laser particle analyzer in a wet state (Mastersizer 2000, Malvern Instruments Ltd., UK). These two samples were mixed with 20 times distilled water for dilution. Then, the mixture was treated by ultrasound at 30 Hz for 5 min for dispersion. Subsequently, the measurement was conducted with the parameters of refractive index and absorbance coefficient at 1.53 and 0.001 respectively. Three runs were performed for each sample. Meanwhile, the particle size D (3, 2) and volume percentage (%) were recorded.

FTIR measurements of the purified TiO2, TK, TKB particles, and grafted starch with and without 4% TKB were carried out on a Nexus 6700 FTIR spectrometer (Nicolet Co., USA). Each sample was scanned 64 times over the 4000–400 cm−1 region at a resolution of 4 cm−1, and the pure potassium bromide was utilized as the background.

The thermal stability of the purified nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB particles was tested by using a thermogravimetric analyzer (TA 2900 from TA Instruments). Samples (5 mg in an alumina pan with a volume of 70 μL) were heated from 25 to 600 °C. The heating rate and nitrogen gas flow were respectively 10 °C/min and 30 mL/min.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Shear strength and rotational viscosity test
ce:section.ce:para: The shear strength test was measured according to our previous report (Chen et al., 2019) using a WDT-10 shear strength analyzer (KQL Co., China), which was based on industry-standard HG/2727-2010 (China 2010). All results are presented as averages of results from 6 independent replicates.

The rotational viscosity after 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 days storage was measured by using an NDJ-8S rotational viscometer (Ping Xuan Shanghai Scientific Instrument Co., China) with No. 4 rotor at a speed of 30 r/min. The testing temperature was 30 °C. All the values were recorded at a stable condition, and the results of rotational viscosity are presented as the averages of 3 independent replicated tests.

All the adhesives with different concentrations of TKB were stored at 25 ± 1 °C and 70% (Relative humidity) RH for 1 day, and then the rheological properties were measured by employing a rheometer (DHR 2, TA Instruments, Crawley, UK) with aluminum parallel plate geometry. The size of the plate was 40 mm and the testing gap was set as 1000 μm. All tests were performed at 25 °C.

The steady (steady shear) and dynamic (frequency sweep and creep recovery) rheological properties were measured at 25 °C according to our previous report (Li et al., 2013). The steady shear measurement was carried out at a range of the shear rate from 0.1 to 300 s−1. For the frequency sweep test, the frequency range was set as 0.1–10 Hz, and the parameter of strain amplitude was selected as 1%. Besides, the creep recovery was firstly measured at a constant stress of 2 Pa within the linear viscoelastic region for 180 s, followed by the recovery period for another 180 s without the constant stress. The yield stress (τ0), fluid consistency (K), and flow index (n) were analyzed by the DRH software, and all the tests were replicated 3 times.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Measurements of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and surface tension (SFT)
ce:section.ce:para: 1 g of each fresh adhesive sample was mixed with 50 distilled water, followed by sonication at 30 Hz for 10 min. Then, a copper grid was immersed in diluted suspension at room temperature in neutral air for drying. Subsequently, the TEM observation was performed through a Hitachi H-7650 TEM Microscope (Tokyo, Japan) at 80 kV.

The surface tension of the adhesives with different TKB contents was measured by using a German Kruss automatic surface tension meter K100 (German KRUSS, Germany). A platinum plate was used as the detector, and the parameters of detection speed, immersion depth, and time were set as 5 mm/min, 2 mm, and 4200 s, respectively. Each sample was measured 3 times.

The grafted starch (6–12 mg) was enclosed into an aluminum pan to measure the glass transition temperature (Tg) using a DSC 200PC (NETZSCH, Germany) under the nitrogen atmosphere. A preheating from 10 to 100 °C (10 °C/min) was performed, and then the temperature range was cooled to 10 °C. Subsequently, the Tg was measured from −70 to 120 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min, and an empty pan was used as a reference.

The Horus® Film Formation analyzer (France) was employed to record the DWS for analyzing the film-forming procedure. The testing method referred to the previous report (Wang et al., 2018). The samples were drawn on an aluminum substrate with a wet thickness of 50 μm, and the wavelength of the testing laser light was 655 nm. The particle diffusion in the drying coating sample was recorded by monitoring the speckle rate during the adhesive film formation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and water contact angles of the latex films
ce:section.ce:para: The latex films were prepared by pouring the adhesive on a Teflon board, and drying the adhesive at 40 °C until a constant weight was achieved. The glued wood veneers with fracture surfaces were collected after shear strength measurement and stored at 25 °C. The surface morphology of the films and wood veneers were observed using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM) with a JSM-630 LV scanning microscope operating at 30 kV. Additionally, the water contact angles of the latex films were measured in a JY-PHa contact angle testing advice (Hebei, China) by dispensing 2 μL water droplets on the surface through the needle tube. These were tested at least at three positions, and the result was calculated from the average values of the measurements.
Statistical analysis was carried out by using the IBM SPSS Statistics 22 (SPSS, Inc. an IBM Company, Chicago, IL, USA).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization analysis of the unmodified and modified nano-TiO2 particles
ce:section.ce:para: Morphology of nano-TiO2 and TKB nanoparticles was observed by TEM. In Fig. 1A , some hard aggregates of untreated TiO2 in the micrometric scale were formed due to the high surface hydrophilicity (-OH). Compared with the nano-TiO2 alone, modified nanoparticles (TKB) exhibited a better dispersion (Fig. 1B). This was attributed to the introduction of KH570 and BA which promoted the surface hydrophobicity and strengthening repulsive forces of the TiO2 nanoparticles. Additionally, TEM images with high resolution of the unmodified and modified TiO2 nanoparticles are presented in Fig. 1A and B. The lattice stripe width (101 Plane) of nano-TiO2 and TKB in Fig. 1 were approximately 0.333 nm and 0.328 nm, respectively. Nevertheless, the coating layer was observed on the surface of TKB, which might be composed of the KH570 and BA (total 2.423 nm) layer. Some previous literature also presented a similar phenomenon as reported in this research (Ni et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2012). Subsequently, the chemical structure of nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB particles was investigated by employing the FTIR spectrum. In Fig. 1C, the new absorption peaks around 1700, 1180, and 420 cm−1 on TK and TKB curves could be respectively assigned to the CO, CO, and SiO groups, demonstrating that KH570 was successfully grafted on the surface of TiO2 particles. In addition, a red shift of -OH peak from 3397 (nano-TiO2) to 3327 cm−1 (TK) suggested that the presence of KH570 facilitated the formation of hydrogen bonds. This could probably be explained by the activated -OH groups on the nano-TiO2 surface before reaction and the hanging -OH groups in the KH570 molecule (Xiang et al., 2015). Besides, compared with the FTIR curve of TK, two stronger adsorption peaks corresponding to the asymmetrical stretching vibration of CH3 and CH2 were noted in the TKB curve at 2925 and 2852 cm−1. Simultaneously, the CH adsorption peak which does not belong to KH570 was also found around 2960 cm−1. These results indicated the presence of BA. After grafting polymerization, a blue shift of -OH peak from 3327 (TK) to 3369 (TKB) cm−1 was observed in Fig. 1D, implying that the coverage of PBA on KH570 limited the surface hydrogen-bonding interaction. This phenomenon could be ascribed to two reasons: (1) an increase in the thickness of the surface layer increased the steric hindrance among particles; (2) the introduction of O-C=O promoted the surface hydrophobic and enhanced the intermolecular repulsion force, leading to the better dispersion of TKB. This was in accordance with the TEM observation. Therefore, the grafting of BA altered the surface properties of nano-TiO2.

TGA is a commonly used method to evaluate the approximate amount of surface modifier coating on the inorganic nanoparticle (Sanchez et al., 2015). Fig. 1E shows the TGA curves of TiO2, TK, and TKB. According to the previous studies, the entire process of the weight loss curve can be divided into two stages. In the water loss stage from 0 to 150 °C (Dan et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013), the weight loss of TK and TKB was significantly less than that of bare TiO2, as the presence of the CC and R-O-C=O groups from KH570 and BA promoted the hydrophobicity of these two samples. Consequently, it was reasonable that there was physical or chemical interaction between the nano-TiO2 and surface modifiers (KH570 and BA). From 150 to 700 °C, TK and TKB exhibited approximately 4.10% and 5.54% weight losses that were related to the combustion of the KH570 and BA on the surface of the TiO2 nanoparticles. There was a 1.44% increase in the weight loss of TKB compared with TK, further demonstrating the successful surface modification.
The survey and high-resolution XPS spectra of nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB were measured to analyze the chemical compositions and conform the grafted reaction on the surface.

In Fig. 2A and B, the full scanning spectral shows the existence of O1s, Ti2p3, Ti2p1, and C1s elements on the surface of the nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB particles. Compared with the untreated nano-TiO2, a new signal peak was observed in the TK and TKB curves at 101.0 eV, which was ascribed to Si2p, implying the presence of KH570. The percentage of these four elements in nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB are listed in Table 1 . When compared with the nano-TiO2 and TK, TKB showed higher C1s and lower O1s percentages as the BA (C7H12O2) contained a high percentage of C atom. Besides, a decrease in the atom percentage of Ti2p and Si2p on the TKB surface was also noted. These results proved the surface coverage of BA.

The high-resolution XPS spectra are also presented in Fig. 2 to evaluate the chemical state of different elements. Fig. 2 shows the detailed spectra of C1s which have been calibrated with a reference C1s peak at 284.8 eV. For the nano-TiO2, the presence of the C1s peak in Fig. 2A and C might be due to the synthesis process. This complex peak can be fitted into three peaks including CC at a binding energy of 284.8 eV, CO at a binding energy of 286.2 eV, and CO at a binding energy of 288.2 eV. However, in addition to those peaks, a weak peak corresponding to CSi was noted in the spectra of TK and TKB at around 283.0 eV, illustrating the presence of KH570. Moreover, the binding energy shift of CO from 288.8 (TK) to 288.7 (TKB) indicated that the addition of BA changed the chemical state of CO on the surface of nano-TiO2. After grafting polymerization, the break of CC and the formation of CC increased the stability of the chemical structure, resulting in lower binding energy. In Fig. 2D, the peak at 529.7 eV was assigned to the O1s in OTi, and the peak at 531.1 eV ascribed to the OH (Kezhen et al., 2016). After surface modification, a new peak at 530.0 eV was observed in both TK and TKB spectra, and the binding energy of O1s peak at 531.2 eV shifted to 531.4 eV due to the break of CC and the introduction of O-C=O. Additionally, Fig. 2E shows the Ti2p XPS spectra containing two peaks at 458.5 eV (Ti2p3) and 462.2 eV (Ti2p1) with a separation of 5.8 eV, which confirmed the presence of the Ti4+ in the oxidation state (Iatsunskyi et al., 2015; Saffar et al., 2014). Furthermore, the Si2p spectra of nano-TiO2, TK, and TKB are also present in Fig. 2F, and the left shift of the Si2p peak was consistent with the above discussion. These results proved that the BA was successfully chemically grafted on the surface of nano-TiO2.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Shear strength and viscosity analysis of starch-based wood adhesive
ce:section.ce:para: The bonding performances of these adhesives containing different percentages of TKB were assessed by measuring the shear strength in dry and wet states.

In Fig. 3A , compared with the control sample, there was no statistically significant change in the dry shear strength of the 2% sample. However, the viscosity of adhesives containing 2% and 4% TKB was lower than that of other groups (Fig. 3B). This phenomenon might be attributed to the surface property of TKB. In the adhesive system, starch would assemble into the latex particles with a shell-core structure after grafting of VAc. Starch and VAc were the shell and core, respectively (Chen et al., 2019). The hydrophobic chains (PBA) could be adsorbed on the surface of latex particles as the VAc grafted onto starch possessed relatively high hydrophobicity. The presence of PBA weakened the molecular interaction and widened the steric hindrance among the latex particles, leading to low viscosity. Meanwhile, TKB with relatively high hydrophobicity displayed better dispersion in adhesive compared with untreated nano-TiO2. This promoted the structural compatibility of adhesives and the mechanical strength of adhesive film (Chen et al., 2006; Giovino et al., 2019).

According to the above discussion, 2% TKB could be well dispersed in the adhesive, and its role might be similar to the surfactant (Maillard et al., 2011). After adding 4% TKB into the sample, the dry shear strength improved by 86.7% to 7.48 MPa. This result could probably be ascribed to the formation of TKB aggregates through the hydrophobic interaction (PBA). This aggregation was likewise similar to the polymer-controlled behavior, but it is a passive behavior caused by the change of concentration (Bilchak et al., 2019). Exposure of hydrophilic surfaces probably facilitated the interfacial contact between the aggregations and starch molecules, resulting in the enhancing structure (Moll et al., 2011).

The trend (0%–4%) of bonding strength was supported by observing the fracture surface of glued wood veneers (Fig. 3D–F). In Fig. 3D, a broken region (red circle) was noted on the wood surface of control sample, indicating that the bonding failure was due to the breaking of wood and adhesive lay. Compared with the control sample, the broken adhesive lay and undamaged wood surface were observed on the 2% wood surface (Fig. 3E). This exactly proved our previous discussion that the lower content of TKB played a similar role as the surfactant in weakening the film cohesiveness. However, for the sample containing 4% TKB, the wood-damaging regions and relatively complete adhesive layer on the wood surface demonstrated that 4% TKB promoted the cohesiveness of latex film. However, at 6% TKB addition, the adhesive's dry shear strength decreased to 5.69 MPa, and the viscosity increased to 3.76 Pa·s. These results might be due to the increasing size of TKB aggregation which reduced the compatibility of the adhesive system. Further incorporation of TKB (8%) broke the interfacial balance between nanoparticle aggregates and latex particles by forming the particle lay. This phase transition shattered the structure of adhesive, leading to lower viscosity and weakened shear strength. Wet shear strength displayed a similar variation trend with the dry shear strength. There was no significant difference in wet shear strength between the control adhesive and adhesive with 2% TKB. However, the adhesive containing 4% TKB showed the highest wet bonding strength at around 1.32 MPa when compared with other samples, which was related to the improved structure and surface properties. When the concentration exceeded 4% TKB, the decline in structural compatibility weakened the resistance of the adhesive system to the absorption of water molecules.

Furthermore, the storage stability of these adhesives was also evaluated by testing the viscosity variation in the storage period as presented in Fig. 3C. The viscosity curves of the adhesives containing 2%, 4%, and 8% TKB were smoother than others, suggesting better storage stability. As mentioned above, 2% TKB weakened the molecular interaction, and 8% TKB broke the phase balance of the adhesive. Moreover, for the adhesive with 6% TKB, TKB aggregates strengthened the structure of adhesive through the non-covalent interaction, leading to the rapidly increasing viscosity. Therefore, the sample containing 4% TKB was concluded to display better bonding and emulsion performances.

It is a well-known fact that bonding strength is determined by the state (liquid and solid) of adhesive. To reveal the molecular mechanism of TKB improving the performance of adhesive in detail, the microstructure and rheological behaviors of the liquid adhesive were subsequently measured.

The nanoparticle aggregation depends on the particle interactions (Tang & Arya, 2017). In this work, the amount of TKB addition might determine the morphology and surface property of latex particle aggregates and subsequently change the performance of the starch-based adhesive. Therefore, the microstructure and surface tension of adhesives containing 0%, 2%, 4% and 6% TKB were, respectively, observed and measured to confirm the foregoing speculation.

In Fig. 4A , the latex particles observed in the TEM image were similar to our previous conclusion (Chen et al., 2019). Compared with the control sample, the latex exhibited a higher dispersion, and only some very small particles were adsorbed on the surface of latex particles (Fig. 4B). Therefore, it was thought that TKB nanoparticles were well dispersed in the adhesive system and enhanced the repulsive force between latex particles. However, when the concentration reached 4%, aggregates with sharp string (red circles) were formed in this adhesive (Fig. 4C). The aggregates served as a sliding bridge, resulting in the formation of a cross-linking region (Fig. 4E).

However, with the increase in the TKB amount (≤6%), several larger latex aggregates and cross-linking areas were observed in Fig. 4D. These results supported our discussion regarding the morphology variations of TKB in the adhesive, and excessive TKB would lead to an unstable adhesive system. In addition to the above-mentioned phenomenons, the adhesives with 2–6% TKB displayed the lower surface tension as shown in Fig. 4, illustrating that the addition of TKB improved the adhesive wettability. The higher surface tension (40.51 mN/m) of 4% adhesive could be attributed to the cross-linking interaction which affected the distribution of molecular weight. Therefore, TKB aggregation played an important role in the adhesive, and moderate aggregation could improve the performance of adhesives.

Steady shear behaviors of the adhesives with different concentrations of TKB are presented in Fig. 5A and D. The variation trend of initially apparent viscosity was similar to the viscosity results, and all the samples showed the typical shear-thinning behavior and pseudoplastic property. It was also found that the Herschel-Bulkley model was the best-fitted model with high coefficients of determination (R2 > 0.999) (Ziaee et al., 2015), and the parameters including yield stress (τ0), fluid consistency (K), and flow index (n) are displayed in Fig. 5B. Compared with the control sample, the addition of TKB reduced the τ0 value from 4.472 (0%) to 1.628 (2%), 2.867 (4%), 3.988 (6%), and 2.952 (8%), suggesting that lower initial yield stress was required for this measurement. This indicated that TKB could weaken the net structure within adhesive, which was consistent with our previous discussion. `Remarkably, the value of τ0 increased with the increasing percentage of TKB from 2% to 6%, and the same trend was also noted for K. This might be due to the variation in the role of TKB which relatively strengthened the net structure but limited the molecular mobility in the starch-based adhesive. When the addition concentration of TKB reached 8%, the over-aggregation of TKB might induce the formation of the large aggregations and nanoparticle layers, again leading to the decrease in τ0 and K. However, the law of n value is not obvious, and the adhesive with 4% TKB showed higher value of n (0.693), probably due to the higher compatibility.

Dynamic rheological properties were further explored by the dynamic oscillatory analysis below to deeply analyze the structural strength of the different samples. In Fig. 5B and E, all the samples showed the frequency dependence, and G′ increased with the increase in frequency. This was partly analogous to the previous reports (Chen et al., 2019). Moreover, the storage module (G′) of each adhesive containing TKB was lower than the control sample, illustrating that TKB was exactly not conducive to the formation of a high-strength structure in the adhesive system. At a very low-frequency range (<0.1 rad/s), G′ of the adhesives increased with the increasing contents of TKB from 2% to 6%. This phenomenon demonstrated that the cross-linking structure was formed in the adhesives with 4% TKB. In the frequency range from 0.1 to 10 rad/s, the G′ curve of the adhesive with 2% TKB showed a steeper increasing trend, probably because of the influence of frequency on the structure of adhesive with TKB. This resulted in that the values of G′ closed to those of the control sample. A similar phenomenon was also noted in the high-frequency range (>10 rad/s) of 4% TKB contained adhesive. This indicated that the cross-linking structure in the adhesives containing 2% and 4% TKB was not sufficient to resist the effect of high frequency. However, the adhesive with 6% TKB displayed a normally increasing trend, probably because the cross-linking interaction in the adhesive enhanced the net structure which could resist the impact of frequency. Further addition of TKB (8%) showed a negative influence on the structure of adhesive, and its G′ values were lower compared with others after 0.1 rad/s.

Fig. 5E exhibits the variations of the loss factor (tan δ) in relation to the angular frequency. Tan δ values of these five samples were less than 1 at the entire frequency range, illustrating the elastic behavior of all the adhesives. It was remarkable that the changing trend was partly different from our previous study (Chen et al., 2018).

At a very low-frequency range (<1 rad/s), it was found that the tan δ of all samples decreased with the increase in frequency. This suggested that low frequency enhanced the elastic behavior of the adhesive. Compared with the control sample, the adhesive with 2%, 4%, 8% TKB showed higher tan δ values under low frequency, indicating that TKB promoted the viscous property. Notably, the viscoelastic behavior of the adhesive with 2% TKB was more susceptible to the frequency. At the middle frequency range (>1 rad/s, <10 rad/s), tan δ values of the adhesives containing TKB were higher than that of the control sample, illustrating that TKB intensified the viscous behavior of adhesive. At the high-frequency range (>10 rad/s), the upward trend of tan δ of all the samples was ascribed to the destruction of the net structure. From the above observation, the adhesives containing 4% and 6% TKB showed high stability at the whole range.

We also measured the creep-recovery curves to further evaluate the structural deformation of the adhesives. In Fig. 5C and F, it was found that the addition of TKB weakened the resistance of adhesives to deformation, and the recovery rate followed the order of 0% ≈ 6% > 4% > 8% > 2%. These results confirmed that TKB could reduce the molecular rigidity and promote the stability of the adhesive system.
The FTIR and DSC measurements were subsequently performed to analyze the chemical structure and thermal behavior of the grafted starch without and with 4% TKB.

In Fig. 6A , the glass transition temperature (Tg) of grafted starch without TKB was at 49.5 °C, and the addition of 4% TKB decreased its Tg to 42.2 °C. This phenomenon was related to the introduction of BA with the lower Tg (Din et al., 2018), and this variation improved the applicability of the adhesive (Wang et al., 2018).

FTIR results are presented in Fig. 6B. For the control sample, a new peak around 1740 cm−1 proved that VAc was successfully grafted on the starch molecules. Additionally, the adsorption peak of -OH displayed a blue shift for adhesive containing 4% TKB, indicating that the addition of TKB inhibited the formation of the hydrogen bond as compared to the control sample. Meanwhile, the absorption peak at around 1620 cm−1 showed a redshift, probably due to the CC group. We also calculated the gap transmittance, ΔT1 (between the peaks around 576 and 1022 cm−1) and ΔT2 (between the peaks around 1620 and 1022 cm−1), to prove the existence of TiO and CC after the normalization. In Fig. 6C, the significantly lower ΔT1 and ΔT2 values of the adhesive with 4% TKB indicated that the amount of these two groups (around 576 and 1620 cm−1) was higher, confirming the successful introduction of TKB.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Microstructure of the adhesive films and water contact angle analysis
ce:section.ce:para: In addition to the preparation and storage of adhesive, the curing of starch-g-PVAc latex particles is also a critical step in the application process (Chen et al., 2018). The grafting of VAc onto starch molecules would alter the film-forming property of starch. Here, to evaluating the impact of TKB on the microstructure of latex film, SEM was employed to observe the surface morphology of the latex film.

In Fig. 7 , the surface of the latex film with 4% TKB (Fig. 7C) was smoother as compared to other samples, indicating better compatibility. However, further addition of TKB (6%) resulted in the rough surface of latex film, due to the formation of the larger aggregation. This phenomenon was also found in Fig. 7E. With the increase in TKB concentration, a large amount of the TKB particles was observed on the surface of the latex film containing 8% TKB, which was related to the migration of TKB aggregates with the water evaporation in this unstable system.

Subsequently, the surface wettability of the latex film was investigated by measuring the contact angle. In Fig. 7, the contact angle increased from 72.37° to 84.45° with the increasing content of TKB from 0% to 4%, implying that the introduction of TKB (2% and 4%) improved the surface hydrophobicity of latex film. By combining the results of SEM in Fig. 7C, the relatively higher contact angle of adhesive with 4% TKB was corresponding to the compact microstructure, and there were few TKB nanoparticles on the surface of these films. Nevertheless, the contact angle decreased to 82.85° when the content of TKB reached 6%. This was due to the low compatibility of the adhesive film with a rough surface. Moreover, the latex film with 8% TKB possessed the largest contact angle, which could be explained by the location of TKB particles (arrow) on the film surface (Fig. E). Therefore, 4% of TKB favored the formation of a film with high compatibility and water resistance.
The film-forming procedure of the adhesives containing different percentages of TKB was tracked by using diffusing wave spectroscopy (DWS), and these results are shown in Fig. 8 .

To accurately analyzing the phase behavior of adhesive in different stages, Fig. 8A displays the signal variations of latex particles diffusing during the whole process including Time-1, Time-2, and Time-3 (three stages) (Brunel & Dihang, 2008; Wang et al., 2018). Time-1, called open time, represents the first point where the fluidity factor reaches 1.3 Hz and shows a sudden drop in the fluidity factor. Before this time, latex particles mainly perform Brownian motion. Time-2 marks the end of packaging when the latex particles are in an ordering process. Time-3 represented the consolidation point, and the deformation of particles and interdiffusion/coalescence processes occurs between the latex particles at this time (Brun et al., 2008).

In Fig. 8B, the addition of TKB prolonged the Time-1 from 8.73 s (0%) to 13.20 (2%), 17.46 (4%), 22.03 (6%), and 14.03s (8%), which might be related to the fact that embedding of nanoparticles limited the evaporation of water. Fig. 8C shows the locations of Time-2 in the 50–800 s period. In this part, Time-2 of adhesive containing 4% TKB was longer than others, indicating that the latex particles in this sample would take more time to reach the packaging level. This phenomenon could be attributed to the tightened structure of the adhesive with 4% TKB. Subsequently, the continuous and hard film would form at Time-3. In Fig. 8D, Time-3 of the 4% sample was shorter than others, suggesting that less time would be taken to form the film at this stage. The fast formation of the adhesive film occurred due to the better compatibility of the components. Moreover, the compact structure of the sample containing 4% TKB retained the higher content of water in the film, resulting in the higher fluidity factor. Once the compact latex film was formed, the cohesive and water resistance would be improved.

In this work, the functional TiO2 nanoparticles were successfully synthesized by surface grafting. It was found that TKB at lower levels was similar to the surfactant resulting in better dispersion but weaker cohesiveness. An increase in TKB formed aggregates and strengthened the latex interaction as the PBA exerted its influence through the bridging effect. These variations in adhesive structure improved the bonding performance, storage stability, and rheological properties. Besides, TKB nanoparticles also altered the water migration rate and film-forming time of the adhesive during the curing process. The film derived from starch-based adhesive with 4% TKB showed higher cohesiveness, a better ability of surface bonding, and better water resistance. This work confirms that the incorporation of surface-functionalized nanoparticles is a valuable option for fabricating high-performance sustainable bio-based adhesives.
